passage: Snow was piling against the lab window in Toronto when Noa saw the draft on the shared screen. Her name sat fourth on the paper, after Hiroshi, the senior researcher, and a student who had attended only two meetings. She had run every experiment, and for six weeks she had also covered Hiroshi's Saturday sessions with undergraduates, "as a learning chance." In the corridor she kept her voice even. "Hiroshi, I would like to talk about the author order and my Saturdays. I'm glad for what you've taught me, and I want the paper to show who did the experiments." He rubbed his neck. "I assumed you were happy to help." She suggested asking the graduate coordinator to look at the contribution list. He hesitated, then nodded. Noa walked back to her bench, her hands still shaking a little.

qa.q: Where was Noa's name on the author list?
qa.a: Her name was fourth on the paper.

qa.q: What might Noa be feeling as she speaks to Hiroshi in the corridor?
qa.a: She is nervous but determined: she keeps her voice even, and her hands are still shaking afterwards.

qa.q: Why was asking the graduate coordinator a sensible step?
qa.a: A neutral person can check the contribution list fairly, so it is not only Noa's word against Hiroshi's.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi see the situation?
qa.a: His remark that he assumed she was happy to help suggests he may not have thought of it as taking her credit and time.

grounding: A guide uses a student's work and time unfairly and she politely names it, sets limits and brings in a neutral person.

passage:
Vidya, you're upset your senior put his name on your poster? Sit. Let me, your Swati mausi, tell you what happened to me.
In 1989 I was twenty-two, a research assistant in a botany lab in Lucknow. For eight months I collected leaf samples from the hills, ran every test, wrote the draft. When the paper came out, my supervisor's name was first, a visiting professor's second, and mine was missing. Not even in the thanks.
I cried in the herbarium. I thought, if I complain, I'm ungrateful. He gave me the job, after all.
My friend Kamla said, "Grateful doesn't mean silent." So I went to him with my notebooks and said, calmly, "Sir, this data is mine. I would like my name on the next version." He blustered. So I took the notebooks to the head of department, who was a fair man.
The correction was printed three months later. My name, second. Protecting your work isn't ungrateful, beta.

qa.q: For how long did Swati collect leaf samples?
Why did Swati hesitate to complain at first?
qa.a: She feared seeming ungrateful because the supervisor had given her the job, and she was hurt enough to cry in the herbarium.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Swati's story, and what did she do?
qa.a: Kamla's words, "Grateful doesn't mean silent"; Swati then spoke calmly to her supervisor with her notebooks, and when he blustered, went to the fair head of department.

qa.q: How did the supervisor react when Swati raised it?
qa.a: He blustered, defensive at being challenged by his assistant.

grounding: Shows a guide taking credit for a junior's work, and naming it politely, then involving someone neutral, without feeling ungrateful.

passage:
The client presentation was at 3 p.m., and at 2:05 Rekha saw the final deck: her market analysis, her charts, three weeks of her evenings, now under "Prepared by Nilesh Joshi". Her laptop was at 9 per cent and the office Wi-Fi kept dropping.
She wanted to storm into the meeting room. She also wanted to say nothing, because Nilesh had trained her, and complaining felt ungrateful.
She did neither. At 2:15 she caught him by the coffee machine. "Nilesh, the analysis section is my work. I'd like my name on those slides and to present that part, or at least be introduced as the analyst."
He frowned. "It's a team effort. Don't make this weird now."
"I'm not. I'm asking politely, and if we disagree I'll ask Kamini ma'am to decide."
He looked at the clock, sighed, and changed the footer on his laptop. In the meeting he said, "Rekha built this section; she'll walk you through it."
Her voice shook on the first slide. By the third it didn't.

qa.q: What did the footer on the deck say?
What two urges did Rekha feel on seeing the deck?
qa.a: Anger that made her want to storm in, and guilt that made her want to stay silent because Nilesh had trained her.

qa.q: How did Rekha protect her work?
qa.a: She named it politely before the meeting, asked for credit and to present, and said she would bring in Kamini ma'am as a neutral person if they disagreed.

qa.q: How did Nilesh first see Rekha's request?
qa.a: As making things "weird" and threatening the team effort, before he gave in and credited her.

grounding: Illustrates a senior using a junior's work without credit, and naming it politely, setting a limit and offering to involve someone neutral.
